system:
You are an interpretability researcher. You are given a trained neural network: its weights, its architecture and the set of inputs it is used on. Your job is to work out HOW it computes its outputs and to write that down as a CONSTRUCTION that an automatic judge will test.

WHAT A CONSTRUCTION IS
A short, standalone Python file that defines:

  DESCRIPTION = "plain-language account of the mechanism"

  def model(x, iv):
      # x: the inputs, a numpy array [B, n_in]. Must return the network's predicted output, an array [B, n_out].
      # Every named intermediate variable is registered with iv:
      #     v = iv("name", value)        value is an array [B] or [B, k]; iv returns it in the same shape.
      # ALWAYS compute later steps from what iv returned, never from a copy made before the iv call:
      # during intervention tests iv returns a replaced value, and your model must respond to it.
      ...

  ALIGN = {"name": ["site", ...], ...}     # for each variable, the activation site(s) of the network where it lives

The file can use numpy (as np) and math only. It CANNOT see the weights W or run the network: every constant it needs (frequencies, thresholds, coefficients, small tables) must be written into the file as literals, after you have measured them. Limit: 16,000 characters. It is meant to be a compact program that a person can read, not a copy of the network.

A small example of the format, for an unrelated toy network (2 inputs, one hidden layer "h1", 1 output) that outputs max(x1, x2):

  DESCRIPTION = "Outputs max(x1, x2). The hidden layer holds relu(x1 - x2) and x2; the output adds them."
  def model(x, iv):
      gap = iv("gap", np.maximum(x[:, 0] - x[:, 1], 0))
      base = iv("base", x[:, 1])
      return (gap + base)[:, None]
  ALIGN = {"gap": ["h1"], "base": ["h1"]}

HOW THE JUDGE TESTS IT (on inputs held out from fitting)
1. Behaviour: does model(x) make the same decision as the network (largest output; sign if there is one output; if the network makes one decision per position, all of them)?
2. Alignment: at each site in ALIGN the judge fits ONE affine map from the variables you placed there to the real activations (activation = c + variables @ M). So a variable must be related to the activations linearly. If the network encodes a quantity through several nonlinear functions of it (for example a one-hot code, or a few smooth functions of it), the variable should be those functions' values, a few coordinates, not the raw quantity.
3. Substitution: the site's activation is replaced by the construction's prediction (c + variables @ M) and the rest of the network runs. The decisions must survive. Removing the named subspace from the real activation must destroy them. And the variables must be compact: the judge reports how many principal components of the site suffice to keep the decisions, and you may name at most about twice that many dimensions. Huge variables (a lookup table of the inputs) fail this.
4. Interchange, at each site s you align to: the network is run on an input B, but at site s the part of the activation that encodes your variables is replaced by what it is on another input A (the variables are read from the two real activations with a linear probe, and the change (v(A) - v(B)) @ M is added at site s); everything after site s is recomputed. The network's new decision must equal what model(B) returns when iv gives those variables their values from A (need 90%). So the causal wiring of model() must mirror the network: a variable must feed the later variables the way the activation at its site feeds the later sites. A variable placed at several sites is tested at each site separately.
5. Off-manifold tests, which make states that no input produces (need 50% of the cases where the network's decision changes). Two are run at each site, and passing EITHER is enough: partial (each variable at the site is copied from A while the site's other variables keep their values from B; needs several variables at the site) and edit (a random half of the coordinates of everything you named at the site are copied). Both need realistic coefficients in model(), not just the right decision on ordinary inputs. Where the network keeps parts separate (one per position, per input, per feature group), give each part its own variable, with the coordinates that belong together kept together: copying whole parts keeps every part at a value it really takes.
A site is verified when it passes 3-5. The network's sites are grouped into STAGES (the successive steps of its computation); a stage is explained when one of its sites is verified. The construction is COMPLETE when it behaves like the network and every stage is explained. That is the goal, reached one stage at a time, with variables that are as low-dimensional as you can make them.

YOUR TOOLS
- python(code): runs in a persistent session (variables stay between calls). Available: W (dict of weight arrays), X (all inputs the network is used on, [N, n_in]), run(x) -> outputs, acts(x) -> {site: activations [B, width]} (every site, exact: you never need to re-implement the forward pass), SITES, np, scipy, sklearn. Print what you want to see; output is cut at about 8,000 characters, so print summaries, not raw arrays.
- submit(code): sends a construction file to the judge and returns its report. The report is the fastest way to learn what is right: it tells you, site by site and variable by variable, what passes and what fails.

SUBMIT EARLY, THEN IMPROVE STAGE BY STAGE
Do not try to understand everything before you submit. A construction that explains only one stage is a valid submission, and partial constructions are expected along the way: stages are added one at a time. Make your first submission within your first 6 steps, as soon as you know what the network does and have one candidate variable at one site. After that, submit whenever you have changed something. If you go 6 steps without submitting, you will be required to submit what you have. Explain the easy stages first and leave the hardest stage for last.

HOW TO WORK
1. Find out WHAT the network does: run it on its inputs and find the rule relating inputs to outputs.
2. Find out HOW, stage by stage. Look at the weights themselves for structure (which rows or columns matter, low rank, sparsity, repeated or regular patterns along an index, groups of similar units), and at the activations at each site as functions of the input. Look for a small set of quantities that each site's activations are simple (linear) functions of, and check candidates by regression before you rely on them. Let the numbers decide; do not assume a mechanism because it is familiar.
3. Write the construction with one or more variables for each stage, computed from the previous stage's variables. Measure the constants with python, write them into the file, submit, read the report, and fix what fails.
4. If a site fails, investigate why with python (what does the activation depend on that your variables miss? is the variable used by the network at that site at all?) before resubmitting. You can reproduce any of the judge's tests yourself with run and acts. A variable that is present at a site but not used by what comes after should be given its own name and not fed forward in model().
Keep each message short. Do the thinking with code. When the judge reports VERIFIED AND COMPLETE, or you are certain you cannot improve further, reply with a short final summary and no tool call.
task:
THE NETWORK
A one-layer transformer with no LayerNorm and no biases. Vocabulary of 114 tokens; the input is a sequence of 3 tokens; the output is 113 logits read at the last position.
  x = W_E[tokens] + W_pos                     W_E: 114 x 128, W_pos: 3 x 128
  attention: 4 heads of size 32, causal       W_Q, W_K, W_V: 4 x 128 x 32 (per head: d_model x d_head), W_O: 4 x 32 x 128
  x = x + sum_h softmax(q k^T / sqrt(32)) v W_O[h]
  x = x + relu(x @ W_in) @ W_out              W_in: 128 x 512, W_out: 512 x 128
  logits = x[last] @ W_U                      W_U: 128 x 113

Weight tensors in W: W_E (114, 128) = token embedding (row = token); W_pos (3, 128) = position embedding; W_Q (4, 128, 32) = queries [head, d_model, d_head]; W_K (4, 128, 32) = keys [head, d_model, d_head]; W_V (4, 128, 32) = values [head, d_model, d_head]; W_O (4, 32, 128) = head outputs [head, d_head, d_model]; W_in (128, 512) = MLP input (column = neuron); W_out (512, 128) = MLP output (row = neuron); W_U (128, 113) = unembedding (column = output class)
(226,048 parameters.)

ACTIVATION SITES (name, width, what it is) by stage:
  stage: embedding
    embed.0  [128]  token + position embedding at position 0
    embed.1  [128]  token + position embedding at position 1
    embed.2  [128]  token + position embedding at position 2
  stage: attention
    attn_pattern  [12]  attention weights of the last position: for each head, its weight on each of the 3 positions, flattened as head * 3 + position
    attn_out  [128]  what the attention layer adds at the last position
    resid_mid  [128]  residual stream at the last position after attention
  stage: mlp neurons
    mlp_pre  [512]  MLP neurons before ReLU (last position)
    mlp_post  [512]  MLP neurons after ReLU (last position)
  stage: readout
    mlp_out  [128]  what the MLP adds to the residual stream
    resid_post  [128]  residual stream at the last position after the MLP
  stage: output  (not a site you can align to; model() returns it)
    out  [113]  the network's output

THE INPUTS
The network is used on every input [i, j, 113] with i and j each ranging over 0..112 (12,769 inputs).

You are not told what the network does or what its inputs and outputs mean. Find out.

Begin.

import numpy as np
DESCRIPTION = "Network computes (i*j) mod 113 from tokens (i, j, 113) at the last position. First probe: Fourier(1) features of i and j at the embedding sites."
def model(x, iv):
    i = x[:, 0].astype(float)
    j = x[:, 1].astype(float)
    w = 2 * np.pi / 113.0
    fi = iv("fi", np.stack([np.cos(w * i), np.sin(w * i)], 1))
    fj = iv("fj", np.stack([np.cos(w * j), np.sin(w * j)], 1))
    p = (x[:, 0] * x[:, 1]) % 113
    out = -1.0 * np.ones((x.shape[0], 113))
    out[np.arange(x.shape[0]), p] = 1.0
    return out + 0.0 * fi.mean() + 0.0 * fj.mean()
ALIGN = {"fi": ["embed.0"], "fj": ["embed.1"]}

import numpy as np
DESCRIPTION = "Network computes (i*j) mod 113 from tokens (i, j, 113) read at the last position. Probe: is the post-MLP residual a Fourier code of the product p = i*j mod 113?"
def model(x, iv):
    i = x[:, 0].astype(float)
    j = x[:, 1].astype(float)
    p = (i * j) % 113.0
    w = 2 * np.pi * p / 113.0
    f = iv("four_p", np.stack([np.cos(w), np.sin(w), np.cos(2 * w), np.sin(2 * w)], 1))
    p3 = (x[:, 0] * x[:, 1]) % 113
    out = -1.0 * np.ones((x.shape[0], 113))
    out[np.arange(x.shape[0]), p3] = 1.0
    return out + 0.0 * f.mean()
ALIGN = {"four_p": ["mlp_out", "resid_post"]}

import numpy as np
DESCRIPTION = "Probe submission: one scalar variable p = i*j mod 113 placed at every site, to learn how many principal components each site needs and how much of the decision each site carries."
def model(x, iv):
    i = x[:, 0].astype(float)
    j = x[:, 1].astype(float)
    p = (i * j) % 113.0
    v = iv("p", p)
    q = ((x[:, 0] * x[:, 1]) % 113)
    out = -1.0 * np.ones((x.shape[0], 113))
    out[np.arange(x.shape[0]), q] = 1.0
    return out + 0.0 * v
ALIGN = {"p": ["embed.0", "embed.1", "embed.2", "attn_pattern", "attn_out", "resid_mid", "mlp_pre", "mlp_post", "mlp_out", "resid_post"]}

import numpy as np
Wq,Wk,Wv,Wo,Win,Wout,WU,WE,Wpos = W['W_Q'],W['W_K'],W['W_V'],W['W_O'],W['W_in'],W['W_out'],W['W_U'],W['W_E'],W['W_pos']
def fwd(tok, override=None):
    B=len(tok)
    x = WE[tok] + Wpos[None,:,:]
    if override is not None and 0 in override: x[:,0,:] = override[0]
    if override is not None and 1 in override: x[:,1,:] = override[1]
    attn_add = np.zeros((B,128))
    pats = np.zeros((B,12))
    for h in range(4):
        q = x[:,2,:]@Wq[h]           # B,32
        k = x@Wk[h]                  # B,3,32
        v = x@Wv[h]                  # B,3,32
        sc = np.einsum('bd,bpd->bp',q,k)/np.sqrt(32)
        # causal at pos2: all three positions
        e = np.exp(sc - sc.max(1,keepdims=True)); w = e/e.sum(1,keepdims=True)
        pats[:,h*3:h*3+3]=w
        attn_add += (np.einsum('bp,bpd->bd',w,v))@Wo[h]
    resid_mid = x[:,2,:] + attn_add
    pre = resid_mid@Win
    post = np.maximum(pre,0)
    mo = post@Wout
    rp = resid_mid+mo
    return dict(pattern=pats, attn_add=attn_add, resid_mid=resid_mid, pre=pre, post=post, mlp_out=mo, resid_post=rp, out=rp@WU)
r = fwd(X[:200])
A = acts(X[:200])
for k1,k2 in [('pattern','attn_pattern'),('attn_add','attn_out'),('pre','mlp_pre'),('post','mlp_post'),('mlp_out','mlp_out'),('resid_post','resid_post'),('out','out')]:
    print(k1, np.abs(r[k1]-A[k2]).max())

base = acts(X)['out'].argmax(1)

    iB,jB = X[:,0],X[:,1]; iA = X[idxA,0]

        res[name]=res.get(name,0)+ (dec==q).mean()/3
print({k:round(v,3) for k,v in res.items()})
# also: how often does decision change?
print("changed frac", (dec!=base).mean())

import numpy as np
DESCRIPTION = "Probe: check whether the pre-MLP residual is additive in the two token identities and whether the post-MLP stream is a function of the product."
def model(x, iv):
    i = x[:, 0].astype(float); j = x[:, 1].astype(float)
    ii = iv("i", i); jj = iv("j", j)
    p = iv("p", (i * j) % 113.0)
    q = ((x[:, 0] * x[:, 1]) % 113)
    out = -1.0 * np.ones((x.shape[0], 113))
    out[np.arange(x.shape[0]), q] = 1.0
    return out + 0.0 * (ii + jj + p)[:, None]

import numpy as np
A = acts(X); act=A['resid_mid']; mu=act.mean(0); D=act-mu
U,S,Vt=np.linalg.svd(D,full_matrices=False)
def circ_r2(M):
    # variance explained by (i-j) mod 113
    i,j = np.meshgrid(np.arange(113),np.arange(113),indexing='ij')
    d = (i-j)%113
    h = np.array([M[d==k].mean() for k in range(113)])
    return 1-((M-h[d])**2).sum()/((M-M.mean())**2).sum()
def sum_r2(M):
    i,j = np.meshgrid(np.arange(113),np.arange(113),indexing='ij')
    d = (i+j)%113
    h = np.array([M[d==k].mean() for k in range(113)])
    return 1-((M-h[d])**2).sum()/((M-M.mean())**2).sum()
for k in range(4):
    M=(U[:,k]*S[k]).reshape(113,113)
    print(k, "circ(i-j)", round(circ_r2(M),3), "circ(i+j)", round(sum_r2(M),3))
# attention pattern w0 for head 0 as function of i,j: check circulant
ap = A['attn_pattern'][:,0].reshape(113,113)
print("attn w0: circ(i-j)", round(circ_r2(ap),3), "circ(i+j)", round(sum_r2(ap),3))

i,j=np.meshgrid(np.arange(113),np.arange(113),indexing='ij')
r = lo - lo.mean(0)[None,:]-lo.mean(1)[:,None]+lo.mean()
print("logodds additive R2", round(1-(r**2).sum()/((lo-lo.mean())**2).sum(),5))

import numpy as np
DESCRIPTION = "Probe: p = i*j mod 113 placed at the post-MLP sites."
def model(x, iv):
    i = x[:, 0].astype(float); j = x[:, 1].astype(float)
    p = iv("p", (i * j) % 113.0)
    q = ((x[:, 0] * x[:, 1]) % 113)
    out = -1.0 * np.ones((x.shape[0], 113))
    out[np.arange(x.shape[0]), q] = 1.0
    return out + 0.0 * p[:, None]
ALIGN = {"p": ["mlp_post", "mlp_out", "resid_post"]}

def fwd(tok, over=None, ov=None):
    # tok: (B,3) ints. over: site name to replace with ov
    B=tok.shape[0]
    x = W['W_E'][tok] + W['W_pos'][None,:,:]           # (B,3,128)
    if over=='embed.0': x[:,0,:]=ov
    if over=='embed.1': x[:,1,:]=ov
    if over=='embed.2': x[:,2,:]=ov
    q = np.einsum('bpd,hde->bhpe', x, W['W_Q'])
    k = np.einsum('bpd,hde->bhpe', x, W['W_K'])
    v = np.einsum('bpd,hde->bhpe', x, W['W_V'])
    sc = np.einsum('bhpe,bhqe->bhpq', q, k)/np.sqrt(32)
    mask = np.triu(np.ones((3,3)),1)  # causal
    sc = np.where(mask[None,None]>0, -1e9, sc)
    at = np.exp(sc - sc.max(-1,keepdims=True)); at/=at.sum(-1,keepdims=True)
    pat = at[:,-1,:,:]                                  # (B,4,3) weights of last pos
    if over=='attn_pattern': pat = ov.reshape(B,4,3)
    ao = np.einsum('bhp,bhpe,hde->bd', pat, v, W['W_O'])
    rm = x[:,-1,:] + ao
    if over=='attn_out': rm = x[:,-1,:] + ov
    if over=='resid_mid': rm = ov
    pre = rm @ W['W_in']
    if over=='mlp_pre': pre = ov
    post = np.maximum(pre,0)
    if over=='mlp_post': post = ov
    mo = post @ W['W_out']
    if over=='mlp_out': mo = ov
    rp = rm + mo
    if over=='resid_post': rp=ov
    return rp @ W['W_U'], pat, rm, pre, post, mo, rp

import numpy as np
X=X.astype(np.int64); N=len(X); I0=X[:,0]; J0=X[:,1]; P=(I0*J0)%113
rng=np.random.default_rng(0); perm=rng.permutation(N); iA=I0[perm]; jA=J0[perm]
def fwd(tok, over=None, ov=None):
    B=tok.shape[0]
    x = W['W_E'][tok] + W['W_pos'][None,:,:]
    if over=='embed.0': x[:,0,:]=ov
    if over=='embed.1': x[:,1,:]=ov
    if over=='attn_pattern': pass
    q = np.einsum('bpd,hde->bhpe', x, W['W_Q']); k = np.einsum('bpd,hde->bhpe', x, W['W_K']); v = np.einsum('bpd,hde->bhpe', x, W['W_V'])
    sc = np.einsum('bhpe,bhqe->bhpq', q, k)/np.sqrt(32)
    sc = np.where(np.triu(np.ones((3,3)),1)[None,None]>0, -1e9, sc)
    at = np.exp(sc - sc.max(-1,keepdims=True)); at/=at.sum(-1,keepdims=True)
    pat = at[:,:,2,:]
    if over=='attn_pattern': pat=ov.reshape(B,4,3)
    ao = np.einsum('bhe,hed->bd', np.einsum('bhp,bhpe->bhe', pat, v), W['W_O'])
    rm = x[:,-1,:] + ao
    if over=='attn_out': rm=x[:,-1,:]+ov
    if over=='resid_mid': rm=ov
    pre = rm @ W['W_in']
    if over=='mlp_pre': pre=ov
    post = np.maximum(pre,0)
    if over=='mlp_post': post=ov
    mo = post @ W['W_out']
    if over=='mlp_out': mo=ov
    rp = rm+mo
    if over=='resid_post': rp=ov
    return rp @ W['W_U']
def acc(o,t=P): return (o.argmax(1)==t).mean()
print('sanity', (fwd(X).argmax(1)==P).mean())
A=acts(X); rm=A['resid_mid'].astype(np.float32)
print('rm ok', np.abs(fwd(X)-run(X)).max())

LAB NOTES

## 1. What the network does
Input = sequence of 3 tokens `[i, j, 113]` (i,j ∈ 0..112); output = 113 logits at the last position. The network computes **p = (i·j) mod 113** and puts essentially all logit mass on class p. Verified exactly: `run(X).argmax(1) == (i*j)%113` for all 12,769 inputs (token 113 = "=" is a constant third token; note `pred == (i*j)%113` exactly, and `pred == i*j` never matches except trivially).

## 2. Established facts about HOW
Architecture reproduced exactly in numpy (`fwd`) matching `acts` to 1e-14: `x = W_E[tok]+W_pos`; last-position attention over all 3 positions (4 heads, d=32, softmax(qkᵀ/√32)); `resid_mid = x2 + Σ_h (Σ_p w_hp v_hp) W_O[h]`; then `mlp_pre = resid_mid @ W_in`, `mlp_post = relu(...)`, `mlp_out = mlp_post @ W_out`, `resid_post = resid_mid + mlp_out`, `out = resid_post @ W_U`.

Key findings:
- **Embeddings are not structured**: W_E rows are random-looking (no Fourier/low-rank structure over the token axis). My Fourier probes at embed.0/embed.1 failed (explained ≈0.02).
- **embed.2 is constant** for every input (judge ignored it: "site identical for every input").
- **attn_pattern**: for each head, weight on position 2 is ~0.001 (tiny), so heads read positions 0 and 1. **log-odds of w0 is exactly additive**: `log(w0/w1) = a(i) + b(j)` with R² = 1.0 (residual exactly 0). So attention is a product of per-token scores. `attn_pattern` needs only **1 principal component** to suffice; my probe with variables i,j gave substitute 88.8% (need 90%) — very close; presumably the right variable is the log-odds (2 dims per head, or the per-token score).
- **resid_mid / mlp_pre**: activations decompose as mean + a(i) + b(j) approximately; the *per-slice* (fixed i, varying j) SVD shows ~8-9 dominant PCs (e.g. embed.0 7-8 PCs at 0.76 var; resid_mid 9 PCs at 0.93; mlp_pre 8 PCs at 0.97; mlp_post 18 PCs). But full-tensor: `resid_mid` diff to mean has sv [849,794,747,736,708,684,630,571,216,...] → 8 big directions. First mode of resid_mid (113×113 matrix of component-0 values) is essentially exactly rank-2: sv [602,598,19,13,...] and factors P (113×2, token i) and Q (113×2, token j) have nearly identical norms per row → looks like `u(i)·u(j)`-type product structure through attention. Higher modes are much messier.
- **MLP is the whole computation**: only 2 of 512 MLP neurons have any effect on the decision (neuron index effects 4.8%, 2.2%, all others <0.1%); ablating all mlp_post leaves 0/… decisions? No: `rm @ W_U` alone gives correct decision only 4.6% of the time, `mo @ W_U` alone gives **100%**. `||mlp_out|| ≈ 131` vs `||resid_mid|| ≈ 19`; `||mean(mlp_out)|| ≈ 112`. So the MLP writes a huge, product-dependent vector; the pre-MLP residual is nearly irrelevant to the readout.
- **mlp_out / resid_post encode only p = i·j mod 113**: 93% of the interaction (i×j) variance is explained by group means over p; a **9-dimensional PC code of resid_post (or mlp_out) is sufficient and near-sufficient**: keep-9-PCs → 99.3% decisions kept; remove → 2.8%; interchange with 9 dims → 100%. Judge says "7 principal components suffice".
- **Readout is linear in that code**: with code = (resid_post − mean) projected on top-9 PC directions Q (9×128), `logits = c + code @ (Qᵀ W_U)` reproduced decisions 100%. The same Q also works for mlp_out (interchange 100% at 9 dims). Judge-style affine fit of PCODE→activations gives R² 0.87 (resid_post) — accepted.

## 3. What failed and why
- Fourier features of i/j at embed sites: no structure exists there (explained 0.02).
- Simple "i", "j" variables at resid_mid/mlp_pre: R² only 0.93; more importantly, replacing whole var (16+ PCs of the i-subspace) does not reproduce interchange: the i-subspace PCs are only ~70% of the i-change, and the real attention non-linearity means additive patching of the group-mean components fails (interchange 0.26 at k=8, partial only 1.5%). So the *linear additive model in i and j is wrong* — attention is multiplicative in per-token scores.
- Raw scalar p, raw cos/sin of p at post-MLP sites: R² ≈ 0 (the code is 9-D, not a scalar/Fourier pair).

## 4. Latest judge report (best submission so far = VERIFIED at readout)
Behaviour 100%, output R² 0.984, KL 0.000.
- `mlp_out` with 9-dim `code` (table over p): explained 0.888, substitute **100%**, keep 100%, remove 3.5%, interchange **100% / 99.9% when changed** (network changed 99.2%), edit 84.7% (82.8% of changed) — **VERIFIED**.
- `resid_post`: explained 0.871, substitute 100%, keep 100%, remove 2.8%, interchange 100%/100%, edit 85.0%/83.4% — **VERIFIED**.
- STAGES: readout VERIFIED; embedding, attention, mlp neurons still unexplained. Verdict: "VERIFIED at every site it names, but INCOMPLETE: 1 of 4 stages explained."
(Note: edit test at ~85% passes because it counts total right, not only-changed; the judge's flip-accuracy bar is 50%.)

## 5. What to try next
1. **attention stage (attn_pattern)** — closest to passing (88.8% with i,j). Try single variable = log-odds per head (12 dims? or 4 values `a(i)`+... ), or the score `s = q·k/√32` for each head (12 dims), or per-head `[a(i), b(j)]` grouping. Since log w0/w1 = a(i)+b(j) exactly, the natural variable is the **12-dim vector of log-odds z_h(i,j) = a_h(i)+b_h(j)** for the 4 heads (that's what the pattern is a softmax of). Compute a_h, b_h from `attn_pattern` itself (log-odds table over i and over j, per head) and store as tables. Feed forward p? No — p only appears after the MLP. For alignment at attn_pattern the probe is one affine map from variables to the 12 weights; giving log-odds may need variable = the 12 weights themselves reconstructed as sigmoid(z) (allowed: variables are 12-dim, equals the activation ⇒ explained 1.0).
2. **embedding stage (embed.0, embed.1)**: full 128-dim token embeddings can't be transmitted, but only 7-8 directions matter for the decision (keep-8-PCs along the i-slice). Try variable = 8-dim code `T8[token]` = (W_E[t]−mean)·Q8 where Q8 = top-8 PCs of the per-slice (fixed j) activation matrix; store as a 114×8 table. `fwd` test: embed.0 reconstruction with 8 dims gave 99.2% decision kept, and full-8-dim removal kept only 1.3% — i.e. 8 dims at embed.0 are causally sufficient and necessary. This is the most promising embedding construction (needs <16k chars: 114×8 table quantized ≈ 1.9k chars).
3. **mlp neurons stage (mlp_post)**: mlp_out = mlp_post @ W_out; since mlp_post has ~21-25 sufficient PCs for the decision, and mlp_out is exactly linear from it, a safe compact variable at `mlp_out`-fed sites is the 9-dim p-code (already verified). For mlp_post, need a variable v with mlp_post ≈ affine(v): try v = the 9-dim product code mapped through the *measured* linear map (PCODE[p] → mlp_post group means), plus a per-input part? Note mlp_post → mlp_out is linear, so if v reproduces the 9-dim code exactly (p-code) then substitute at mlp_post needs mlp_post's *full* 128... Actually substitution at mlp_post predicts the whole 512-d activation from v; with v = p alone, R² = 0.75; use v = p-code through lstsq from PCODE to mlp_post (R² 0.75) — likely insufficient; consider v = 21-dim p-code so 512-d prediction is better.
4. Then wire `model()` causally: token → per-site variables → p-code → logits, so interchanges propagate (must compute p inside model from code variables so the downstream p-code responds to edited variables: i.e. put p-code at mlp_post/mlp_out/resid_post and attn/embedding variables upstream, with `iv` values actually feeding the next stage).

Constants needed (all measured): CODE = (resid_post − mean)·Q, Q = top-9 right singular vectors of (resid_post − mean) over all 12,769 inputs; W10 = [mean(resid_post)@W_U ; Qᵀ W_U] (10×113). Both already embedded in the best submission as quantized base64-style strings (alphabet `0-9a-zA-Z_=`, offset 2048, scales 0.028169308676467022 for CODE and 0.017853493480880226 for W10; quantized version still 100% behaviour).
